# Worked examples: code {#sec-examples-code}

```{r}
source("R/book.R")
ex1 <- read_example("ex01_fleet_2022")
ex2 <- read_example("ex02_fiesta_mileage_by_age")
ex3 <- read_example("ex03_co2_recorded_vs_filled")
ex4 <- read_example("ex04_cohort_status")
ex5 <- read_example("ex05_where_did_they_go")
pca_names <- read_pipeline("inputs", "postcode_area_names.csv")
```

These examples query the vehicle table with DuckDB SQL. Run them from R,
Python or the command line as shown in @sec-getting-started, replacing
`vehicles_enhanced.parquet` with the path to your copy. The results shown are
from running exactly these queries on the current version of the data. The
queries are kept in the book's [`sql/`](https://github.com/CARS-Project/documentation/tree/main/sql)
folder.

## Example 1: counting the vehicles observed in a year

**Question:** How many vehicles of each type and fuel were observed in 2022?

```sql
{{< include ../sql/ex01_fleet_2022.sql >}}
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-code-ex1
#| tbl-cap: "Vehicles observed in 2022, by body type and fuel group (largest ten groups)."
kable(head(ex1, 10), row.names = FALSE)
```

The key step is the `WHERE` clause. Without it, the count would include every
vehicle in the table, including those scrapped in 2006 and those not yet
built in 2022.

## Example 2: reshaping to one row per vehicle per year

**Question:** How does the annual mileage of a Ford Fiesta change as it ages,
and has that changed over time?

The vehicle table has one column per year. To analyse by age, the year
columns need to become rows. DuckDB's `UNPIVOT` does this: the mileage and
plausibility columns are unpivoted separately and joined back together by
vehicle and year. Filtering to one model first keeps the reshaped table
small.

```sql
{{< include ../sql/ex02_fiesta_mileage_by_age.sql >}}
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-code-ex2
#| fig-cap: "Average annual mileage of Ford Fiestas by age, plausible mileage only."
ex2$year <- factor(ex2$year)
ggplot(ex2, aes(age, mean_mileage, colour = year)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = cars_cols) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma(), limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Miles per year") +
  theme_cars()
```

Mileage falls with age, and the whole curve is lower in 2022 than in 2010.
Note that the youngest ages are missing: Fiestas under three have no MOT. The
mileage at age 3 averages the whole period since new.

## Example 3: recorded against filled values

**Question:** Does the CO~2~ of new petrol and diesel cars depend on whether
the value was recorded or filled from similar vehicles?

`co2_src` records where each harmonised value came from. Comparing the
average of all values with the average of recorded values only is a quick
test of whether filling gaps has changed a result.

```sql
{{< include ../sql/ex03_co2_recorded_vs_filled.sql >}}
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-code-ex3
#| tbl-cap: "Average CO~2~ (g/km) of cars by year of first use: all values, and recorded values only."
kable(ex3, row.names = FALSE,
      col.names = c("First used", "Fuel", "With CO2", "Mean, all",
                    "Recorded", "Mean, recorded"))
```

Here the two averages are almost identical, because most cars of these years
have a recorded value. Note the rise after 2017 for both fuels: this coincides
with the change from the NEDC to the WLTP test (@sec-fuels-emissions), not
necessarily a real increase.

## Example 4: following a cohort

**Question:** What happened to the cars first used in 2008?

```sql
{{< include ../sql/ex04_cohort_status.sql >}}
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-code-ex4
#| fig-cap: "Cars first used in 2008, by their status in each year."
ex4$status <- factor(ex4$status,
                     levels = c("observed", "unknown", "dead", "unborn"),
                     labels = c("Observed", "Unknown", "Dead", "Unborn"))
ggplot(subset(ex4, year >= 2008), aes(year, n_vehicles, colour = status)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = cars_cols) +
  scale_y_count() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Cars") +
  theme_cars()
```

The cohort is almost all `unknown` until 2011, when most cars have their
first MOT; it is then observed every year and gradually becomes `dead` as cars
stop being tested. A small number are observed before 2011: cars tested early,
such as taxis. The `unknown` line rises again at the end of the series: cars
that may simply not have been tested *yet* (@sec-pitfalls, pitfall 4).

## Example 5: where vehicles go

**Question:** Of the cars tested in the Leeds postcode area in 2019, where
were they four years later?

```sql
{{< include ../sql/ex05_where_did_they_go.sql >}}
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-code-ex5
#| tbl-cap: "Where cars tested in Leeds (LS) in 2019 were in 2023."
r <- merge(ex5, pca_names, by.x = "pca_2023", by.y = "pca", all.x = TRUE,
           sort = FALSE)
r <- r[order(-r$n_vehicles), ]
r$Area <- ifelse(is.na(r$area_name), r$pca_2023,
                 paste0(r$area_name, " (", r$pca_2023, ")"))
r$Share <- fmt_pct(r$n_vehicles / sum(r$n_vehicles))
kable(r[, c("Area", "n_vehicles", "Share")], row.names = FALSE,
      col.names = c("2023", "Cars", "Share of those shown"))
```

Most were still tested in Leeds, and most of the rest had stopped being
tested or were tested in a neighbouring area (Bradford, Wakefield, Sheffield,
York). Moves to neighbouring areas will include cars that simply changed
garage.
